title: Episode 168: Warren G. Harding and the Return to Normalcy: The Smoke-Filled Room (1920–1921)
description:
Exhausted by World War I, racial violence, the Spanish flu epidemic, and Woodrow Wilson's moral crusades, the American people in 1920 longed for a restoration of peace and simplicity. Enter Warren Gamaliel Harding—a tall, handsome, silver-haired small-town newspaper publisher from Marion, Ohio, with a booming baritone voice and a genial disposition. Emerging from the legendary midnight 'smoke-filled room' in Suite 404 of Chicago's Blackstone Hotel, Harding coined the immortal phrase that captured the national soul: 'America's present need is not heroics, but healing; not nostrums, but normalcy.' Conducting a folksy Front Porch Campaign, Harding scored the largest popular landslide in American history up to that time. Discover the forgotten charm and genuine promise of Warren G. Harding.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we step into the dawn of the Roaring Twenties with Warren G. Harding. Handsome, modest, and extraordinarily genial, Harding was the anti-Wilson: a small-town Ohio publisher who promised to lower taxes, restore business confidence, and let the American people heal after years of global war. Here is George with the full story of the Return to Normalcy.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE MAN FROM MARION
Warren Gamaliel Harding looked more like a President of the United States than any man who ever lived. Standing over six feet tall with broad athletic shoulders, a mane of distinguished silver hair, striking hazel eyes, and a deep, resonant baritone voice, Harding was the living portrait of classical American dignity. Born in Corsica, Ohio, in 1865, the son of a country doctor, Harding grew up in rural modesty, learning the printing trade as a barefoot teenager by setting lead type and operating manual press levers.\n\nAt age nineteen, Harding pooled his meager savings with two friends to purchase the failing Marion Daily Star newspaper for three hundred dollars. Through sheer hard work and a sunny, warm disposition, Harding turned the Star into one of the most prosperous and beloved small-town daily newspapers in Ohio. Harding loved small-town life: he played the sousaphone in the Marion Citizens' Cornet Band, joined the Elks, the Odd Fellows, and the Rotary Club, and treated every townsperson as a personal friend. He married Florence Kling DeWolfe—a formidable, razor-sharp businesswoman nicknamed 'The Duchess'—who managed the newspaper's finances with iron discipline while consulting professional astrologers to guide her handsome husband's political career. Harding's genial, handsome demeanor and down-to-earth Midwestern charm offered an irresistible contrast to the exhausting moral crusades and wartime sacrifices of the Wilson years. Harding's easygoing, handsome presence seemed to promise an era of comforting domestic tranquility after a decade of war, ideological fervor, and global upheaval.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE SMOKE-FILLED ROOM AT THE BLACKSTONE
Elected to the United States Senate in 1914, Harding proved to be an affable, well-liked lawmaker who rarely made waves, loved all-night poker games, and avoided ideological battles. In June 1920, the Republican National Convention met in Chicago under stifling, ninety-degree heat. The convention deadlocked in a venomous stalemate between General Leonard Wood and Illinois Governor Frank Lowden. Ballot after ballot passed without a victor.\n\nAround two o'clock in the morning on Saturday, June 12, a cabal of powerful Republican senators and party bosses gathered in Suite 404 of the Blackstone Hotel. Through a dense haze of cigar and cigarette smoke, the bosses searched for an acceptable compromise candidate who had made no enemies and would cooperate with Congress. Harry M. Daugherty, Harding's clever political manager, had predicted the exact scenario months earlier: 'At two o'clock in the morning, fifteen men in a smoke-filled room will agree on Harding.' Around five in the morning, the bosses summoned Harding to the suite, asked him if there was any scandal in his past that would embarrass the party, and upon his reassurance, threw their support behind him. On the tenth ballot that afternoon, Warren G. Harding was nominated for President of the United States. That midnight meeting in the smoke-filled suite of the Blackstone Hotel became the legendary archetype of backroom party boss politics, selecting a consensus candidate who would prove disastrously loyal to corrupt friends. The backroom machinations at the Blackstone Hotel revealed the pragmatic reality of party machinery, where electability and amiability often trumped rigorous intellectual depth.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE GOSPEL OF NORMALCY
In 1920, the American electorate was profoundly exhausted. The trauma of World War I, the terror of the Red Scare, bloody race riots in Chicago and Washington, a wave of violent labor strikes, and the moral lecturing of Woodrow Wilson had left the nation craving tranquility. Harding understood the psychological mood of the country better than any politician in America. In a speech to the Home Market Club in Boston, Harding coined an ungrammatical word that became the defining anthem of the decade:\n\n'America's present need is not heroics, but healing; not nostrums, but normalcy; not revolution, but restoration; not agitation, but adjustment; not surgery, but serenity; not the dramatic, but the dispassionate; not experiment, but equipoise; not submergence in internationality, but sustainment in triumphant nationality.' Critics and English professors mocked the word 'normalcy' as an ignorant bastardization of 'normality,' but ordinary citizens embraced it with relief. To a battered nation, normalcy meant peace, modesty, lower taxes, and the freedom to live their private lives without federal interference. The pledge of a 'return to normalcy' captured the deep longing of an anxious, post-pandemic nation for calm, predictable stability and economic revitalization. Normalcy was not a retreat from greatness, but a collective sigh of relief from an electorate that wanted government to leave them alone to build homes, farms, and businesses.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE FRONT PORCH OF 1920
Following the successful model of his Ohio mentor William McKinley, Harding conducted a charming, folksy 'Front Porch Campaign' from his home on Mount Vernon Avenue in Marion. While Democratic nominee James M. Cox and his thirty-eight-year-old running mate, Assistant Secretary of the Navy Franklin Delano Roosevelt, traveled twenty thousand miles exhausting themselves on campaign trains, Harding stayed on his front lawn. Over six hundred thousand visitors—delegations of farmers, factory hands, suffragists, and movie stars like Al Jolson and Mary Pickford—traveled to Marion to shake Harding's hand.\n\nFlorence Harding baked thousand-mile cookies for visitors, and Harding's beloved Airedale terrier, Laddie Boy, greeted reporters on the porch. The 1920 election was also the first presidential election in which women across all forty-eight states exercised the right to vote under the newly ratified Nineteenth Amendment. On November 2, 1920—Harding's fifty-fifth birthday—the voters rendered a verdict of staggering finality. Harding won 60.3 percent of the popular vote, defeating Cox by over seven million votes—the largest popular landslide in American history up to that time, carrying every state outside the Solid South. Harding's front porch campaign in Marion, Ohio, recalled the folksy traditions of William McKinley, welcoming ordinary citizens with warm handshake diplomacy and modest hospitality. The Marion front porch campaign demonstrated the enduring appeal of traditional, neighborly politics in an age of rapid technological and social change.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE BEST MINDS AND THE WORST HACKS
Taking office in March 1921, Harding possessed a humble, realistic understanding of his own limitations: 'I am a man of limited talents from a small town,' Harding admitted to friends. 'I must surround myself with the best minds in the country.' In many respects, Harding assembled one of the most brilliant cabinets in American history. He named Charles Evans Hughes as Secretary of State, Herbert Hoover as Secretary of Commerce, and billionaire industrialist Andrew W. Mellon as Secretary of the Treasury. Together, these men revolutionized federal administration: Mellon slashed taxes and balanced the budget; Hoover modernized aviation and radio regulation, and Hughes negotiated the historic Washington Naval Treaty of 1922, which resulted in the scrapping of nearly two million tons of warships and averted a naval arms race in the Pacific.\n\nYet Harding possessed a fatal, tragic character flaw: he could never say no to his personal friends. Alongside the 'best minds,' Harding brought a corrupt gang of small-town Ohio political cronies to Washington—the notorious 'Ohio Gang.' He appointed his political manager Harry Daugherty as Attorney General, his poker-playing buddy Albert B. Fall as Secretary of the Interior, and a charismatic, corrupt deserter named Charles R. Forbes as director of the newly created Veterans' Bureau. While Harding worked diligently in the Oval Office, the Ohio Gang set up a corrupt headquarters in a green house on K Street, peddling pardons, bootlegging permits, and government contracts for millions of dollars in bribes. His landslide victory in 1920 was the most lopsided popular mandate in a century, reflecting the American public's decisive repudiation of international entanglements and federal overreach. The overwhelming mandate of 1920 reflected a widespread desire to focus on domestic economic expansion, job creation, and industrial modernization.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE PROGRESSIVE COURAGE OF AN OHIO CONSERVATIVE
Despite the corruption gathering in the shadows, Harding's personal leadership was marked by surprising moments of remarkable moral courage. In October 1921, Harding traveled to Birmingham, Alabama, to deliver a major address celebrating the city's semi-centennial. Standing before an audience of thirty thousand white and Black citizens separated by a wire fence, Harding did something no sitting American president had dared to do since Reconstruction.\n\nLooking into the sea of hostile white faces, Harding demanded full political and economic equality for African Americans: 'Let the Black man vote when he is fit to vote; let the white man vote when he is fit to vote... I want to see the time come when Black men will regard themselves as full participants in the American system, entitled to equal economic and educational opportunity.' A stunned, icy silence fell over the white audience, while Black spectators cheered wildly from behind the wire fence. Furthermore, on Christmas Day of 1921, Harding demonstrated profound magnanimity by commuting the prison sentence of Socialist leader Eugene V. Debs, who had been imprisoned under Wilson for anti-war speeches, inviting Debs to the White House for a warm, cordial private chat. Harding took genuine pride in appointing stellar statesmen like Charles Evans Hughes and Herbert Hoover to his cabinet, genuinely hoping to preside over an era of honest, competent administration. His administration oversaw significant early achievements, including the Washington Naval Conference that successfully limited naval armaments among world powers.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE DARK CLOUD GATHERS
By the spring of 1923, the walls were beginning to close in on Warren G. Harding. The economy had rebounded with roaring vitality: unemployment had vanished, factories were humming, and the Roaring Twenties were in full swing. But whispers of systemic corruption inside his administration began reaching the President's desk. Harding learned that Charles R. Forbes had looted over two hundred million dollars from the Veterans' Bureau, selling hospital supplies and pocketing kickbacks from contractors.\n\nHarding summoned Forbes to the White House, seized the corrupt director by the throat in the bedroom, and shook him with terrifying fury: 'You yellow-bellied scoundrel! You sold out your country!' Harding allowed Forbes to flee to Europe and resign, but the betrayal broke Harding's heart. Rumors were also circulating about secret oil leases in Wyoming and California handled by Secretary Fall. Harding looked at his trusted friend William Allen White and confessed his profound despair: 'My God, this is a hell of a job! I have no trouble with my enemies... but my damn friends, White, my damn friends! They're the ones that keep me walking the floor nights!' Exhausted, sleepless, and suffering from advanced heart disease, Warren G. Harding prepared to embark on a cross-country 'Voyage of Understanding' to Alaska—a journey from which he would never return alive. Yet in surrounding himself with corrupt poker-playing cronies from Ohio, Harding unwittingly welcomed a den of thieves into the highest councils of the federal government. But the presence of corrupt opportunists in his inner circle was an insidious rot that would ultimately destroy Harding's peace of mind and historical legacy.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Warren G. Harding brought peace, healing, and prosperity to an exhausted nation, yet his blind loyalty to corrupt friends would cast an enduring shadow over his name. Next week, we examine the shocking climax of Harding's presidency: the Teapot Dome scandal, the voyage to Alaska, and the mysterious death in a San Francisco hotel suite that shocked the world. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
